newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: High U.S. prices turn away Philippine grain buyers.
newsitem.headline: High U.S. prices turn away Philippine grain buyers.

text.p: Philippine grains importers are expected to shy away from the U.S. market and shift to other sources of wheat and soybeans if prices remain at current high levels next week, traders said on Friday.
"We are actually reviewing the offer for Canadian wheat and South American soybean due to high prices in the United States," said an official at a local flour miller.
A Philippine firm rejected on Friday tenders for 23,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat and 15,000 tonnes of soybeans due to high prices. Both commodities are for April and May deliveries.
Traders said U.S. wheat is now trading around $194 to $196 a tonne C&F while soybeans are trading at $340 to $345 a tonne.

On March 7, a Philippine firm bought 15,000 tonnes of western white wheat at $3.70 per bushel FOB U.S. Pacific northwest port The firm also bought 25,000 tonnes of dark northern spring wheat with 14 percent protein content at $3.90 a bushel.
Traders said other firms have also started to scout for suppliers for their April and May requirements.
Philippine firms buy most of their wheat and soybean requirement from the United States.
Canadian wheat suppliers have assured Philippine buyers that the port congestion in the port of Vancouver due to weather problems had eased.
Last month, Philippine mills that bought Canadian wheat for February and March deliveries sought price cuts from the suppliers due to delayed shipments.
Philippine soybean buyers are also expected to flock to South America, which is expected to harvest a bumper soybean crop this year, in their search for lower prices.
The country's soymeal imports in 1997 are likely to rise to 1.4 million tonnes from last year's 1.2 million.
Philippine firms buy an average of 20,000 tonnes of soybean a month.
In 1996, the Philippines bought about 55 percent of its soybean and soymeal from the United States and 30 percent from Brazil. The remainder came from India, Argentina and China.
Prices of local flour remained steady at 290 pesos per 25-kg for hard flour and 260 pesos per 25 kg for soft flour.
Meanwhile, Manila traders said they expected a rest on rice and corn importations this week as the state-owned National Food Authority's orders in the past several weeks started to arrive.
The NFA said a ship with a cargo of 12,738 tonnes of U.S. rice arrived in the country on March 6 while another ship containing 36,981 tonnes of yellow corn from China arrived on Thursday.
The NFA bought 650,000 tonnes or rice from China, Vietnam, Thailand and Malaysia and 120,000 tonnes of corn from China in the past several weeks to beef up the country's stocks.
The average price of yellow corn in the local market rose to 10.79 pesos per kg while a kg of white corn slipped to 10.94 pesos per kg from 10.95.
